slides.title: One person cannot scale execution - until the architecture changes
bullets: Every task you do yourself is a task you cannot parallelize, and a company is a queue of tasks.
Cloud APIs meter every thought, so iteration gets taxed and agents learn to be stingy.
Business data, credentials, and client material deserve to stay on your own machine.
The answer is not a smarter chatbot; it is an operating system that routes, remembers, and enforces.
slides.note: ZalinOS was designed as infrastructure, not as a demo.

slides.title: The bottleneck was never model intelligence - it was context quality
slides.insight: The same 7B model produced mediocre output with vague context and excellent output with structured memory.
slides.note: Task-quality index, illustrative - consistent with six months of production behavior.

slides.title: Structured memory, not a text dump
bullets: Rules are binding and append-only: true until changed, versioned, never silently edited.
Status is current truth: overwritten constantly, always what is happening right now.
Lessons are incident reports: what broke, why, and the fix, attached to evidence.
Every agent reads all three before starting work, so every session starts with the full picture.
slides.note: Retrieval gives you text that looks relevant; structure gives you facts that are current.

slides.title: A day of agent work is mostly well-specified, repeatable work
slides.insight: That is exactly the work agents do reliably - and exactly the work that used to consume the founder.
slides.note: Illustrative effort distribution across the 9-agent workforce.

slides.title: Four gates plus one rule: a blocker stops the line
rows: The single most important user journey works end-to-end
If it breaks, the build does not ship
Every interactive element does what it claims
Anything that lies is fixed or removed
Version increments and the previous build is archived
Rollback is routine, not an emergency
A log, file, or marker a stranger could audit
A status field is not evidence
One blocked item means no deploy
slides.note: Gates turn machine-speed output from a liability into an asset.

slides.title: Routing accuracy is a number, read after every change
slides.insight: Fewer categories with sharper edges took a small local model to 100% on 30 real queries.
slides.note: Production today: 51/52 automated checks passing; the single miss was a genuinely ambiguous query.

slides.title: Local-first is a decision, not a religion

left.title: What local-first gives up
bullets: The frontier-model ceiling on the hardest reasoning tasks
Hardware planning becomes your responsibility
Vendor conveniences you now build yourself

right.title: What it buys back
bullets: Flat cost: iteration is free, so agents re-check and document freely
Privacy: business data never leaves the machine
Reliability: no rate limits and no 2 a.m. deprecations

slides.note: For an always-on operational workforce, the trade is not close.

slides.title: Nine scoped agents beat one generalist
bullets: Engineering agents build and maintain apps end-to-end, from structured specs to shipped builds.
QA, PM, and Docs agents enforce the gate, track status, and make sure the company never forgets.
Specialists cover data, GIS, OSINT, and system watching, using public data with strict provenance.
Every agent has a scoped mandate, its own queue, and the same shared memory.
slides.note: A general chatbot can attempt anything; a scoped agent does one thing repeatably.

slides.title: What building an agent OS actually taught me
bullets: Routing is the real intelligence: a small model with an excellent router beats a giant model guessing.
Free-form memory rots; structured memory compounds, because format is governance.
Prompts are suggestions and protocols are law: binding, versioned rules outlive phrasing.
Design the system so intelligence is fungible, and the model brand stops mattering.
slides.note: The intelligence ceiling matters less than the system design around it.

bullets: I design and build local-first AI agent systems, from routing and memory to quality gates.

decks.title: Web Scraping Toolkit: Pipelines That Survive the Real Web
decks.subtitle: Scraping is not a script. It is a small system you operate.
decks.desc: A 4,398-line open-source toolkit for collection pipelines that survive markup drift, bot walls, and regional quirks - validated on every run, polite by design, and logged so humans can audit them.

slides.title: Web Scraping Toolkit
slides.subtitle: Pipelines that survive contact with the real web

slides.title: What this deck covers
items: Why the real web breaks naive scrapers every month
Five instrumented stages of a collection pipeline
Validating every run: counts, schema, and sanity ranges
Tolerant extraction, polite crawling, and logs a human can read
What the toolkit delivers in production engagements

slides.title: The real web is hostile
bullets: Markup drifts and selectors rot silently while the script still exits zero.
Bot walls evolve weekly, and yesterday's headers are today's block.
Pages render differently by region, device, and language.
Every freelance client has heard the same story: the script worked last month and now returns nothing.
A script that worked once is not a system - and the web punishes scripts.
slides.note: The failure mode that hurts clients most is silence, not the crash.

slides.title: Five stages, all instrumented

steps.title: Crawl
steps.text: Polite, rate-limited, and resumable - the run can stop and continue.

steps.title: Extract
steps.text: Structural anchors with multiple fallbacks instead of brittle selectors.

steps.title: Validate
steps.text: Row counts, schema, and sanity ranges checked on every single run.

steps.title: Store
steps.text: Clean shapes that downstream tools want, not raw scrapings.

steps.title: Monitor
steps.text: Freshness alarms and structured logs instead of silent deaths.

slides.note: Every stage records what it did - nothing about a run is a mystery.

slides.title: One framework, four disciplines

kpis.label: Lines of code
kpis.sub: Open source and production-tested across client engagements.

kpis.label: Core principles
kpis.sub: Validate every run, tolerate extraction, stay polite, log for humans.

kpis.label: Runs validated
kpis.sub: No run is trusted just because it exited zero.

kpis.label: Credentials used
kpis.sub: Public data only - no logins, no pretending.

slides.note: Built for engagements where the data has to keep arriving, month after month.

slides.title: Validate every run
bullets: A scraper that silently returns empty data is worse than one that crashes loudly.
Row counts are compared against expectations on every execution.
Schema validation catches the column that quietly disappeared.
Sanity ranges catch the price that came back as zero or a million.
Validation turns 'I think the data arrived' into evidence it did.
slides.note: Do not trust a run because it exited zero.

slides.title: What run validation catches before clients do
slides.insight: Validation catches the boring failures first - the ones that would otherwise become next week's emergency.
slides.note: Illustrative mix across monitored engagements; the point is the coverage, not the exact counts.

slides.title: Tolerant extraction beats perfect selectors
bullets: Exact CSS selectors are a liability - they rot the first time a site redesigns.
Structural anchors survive markup changes that kill position-based paths.
Multiple fallbacks degrade gracefully instead of failing completely.
Partial data with a warning beats zero data with a shrug.
Every degraded run is flagged, so partial never masquerades as complete.
slides.note: Extraction is designed to lose a limb, not the whole pipeline.

slides.title: Extraction outcomes across a monitored run
slides.insight: Partial data with a warning beats zero data with a shrug - the pipeline degrades, it does not die.

items.label: Hour 0
items.title: Detection
items.text: Validation flags a row-count drop the day the site changes - not when a client calls.

items.label: Hour 0
items.title: Containment
items.text: Fallback selectors keep extracting while the primary path is broken.

items.label: Hour 1
items.title: Diagnosis
items.text: Structured run logs point straight at the anchor that moved.

items.label: Day 1
items.title: Fix
items.text: The patched selector ships as a normal code change, not an archaeology dig.

items.label: Day 1
items.title: Verification
items.text: The next runs return to clean extraction, and the incident is logged.

slides.note: Sites will change - the system is designed around that certainty.

slides.title: A script you hope for vs a system you operate

left.title: Script
bullets: Written once, then prayed over
Fails loudly, or worse, returns empty
Debugging means scrolling terminal history
Nobody knows it broke until the data is wrong

right.title: System
bullets: Validated on every run with defined expectations
Degrades gracefully and flags partial results
Structured logs: fetched, skipped, doubted
Freshness alarms page a human before the damage

slides.note: Clients do not buy scrapers - they buy data that keeps arriving.

slides.title: Be a polite guest
bullets: Robots directives and terms of service are respected, not negotiated.
Rate-limiting is self-imposed before sites have to impose it.
Only public data is collected - no credentials, no pretending to be a user.
Sustainable scraping is slow, boring, and ethical - and it is the only kind that lasts.
Politeness is not just ethics; it is what keeps access working for months.
slides.note: Ethical collection is a feature clients can put their name on.

The golden path check is boring, repeatable, and non-negotiable; that is exactly why it works.
Gate 2: agents sweep every screen so every button, link, and toggle does what it claims or gets removed.
An interactive element that lies is a bug, full stop - and offline behavior gets checked too.
slides.note: One most-important journey, swept screens, zero exceptions.

slides.title: What a dead-button sweep actually catches
slides.insight: The most common finding is an element that renders perfectly and does nothing - invisible to a passing test suite, obvious to a sweep.
slides.note: Illustrative incident mix consistent with agent screen sweeps across 30+ apps.

slides.title: Version-and-backup and physical evidence
bullets: Gate 3: no release without a version increment, and the previous version is archived before the new one ships.
Rollback is a normal Tuesday, not an emergency - this one rule has saved more projects than any clever architecture.
Gate 4: passing means a log, a file, a screenshot, or a marker - something a stranger could audit.
A status field is not evidence; agents behave differently when they know someone will check the artifacts.
slides.note: Archive first, promote second - the previous version is always one step away.

slides.title: Gates front-load the pain, then the escapes go to zero
slides.insight: Early releases catch the most, and escapes trend to zero as specs and sweeps mature - the gate gets smarter with every run.
slides.note: Illustrative trend for one app's first six gated releases; the point is the direction, not the decimals.

slides.title: A gate that cannot stop traffic is not a gate
bullets: One blocked item equals no deploy - the gate is only real if it can stop the line.
No 'just this once': exceptions are how gates die, quietly and permanently.
Agents never approve their own releases - flagged decisions route through a human approval queue.
Evidence is recorded where reviewers can actually find it, not scattered across chats.
slides.note: Make honesty cheaper than lying, and the easy path becomes the correct path.

slides.title: ETL fails quietly
bullets: Silent truncation, schema drift, and stale schedules never announce themselves.
Nobody notices for weeks - then leadership quotes the wrong number in a meeting.
The pipeline that 'works' is the most dangerous one, because nobody checks it.
Loud failures get fixed the same day; quiet failures get fixed never.
The design goal is not fewer failures - it is failures that cannot stay silent.
slides.note: Every principle in this playbook exists to make failure loud.

slides.title: Profile sources before you trust them
bullets: Every source gets a profile: expected row counts, key uniqueness, update cadence.
Known quirks are documented per source, next to the pipeline that consumes it.
Restated numbers, skipped Sundays, late posts - every source has a personality.
Profiling turns 'the data is wrong' into 'this feed always restates yesterday'.
Half of quality issues are simply behavior nobody wrote down.
slides.note: You cannot validate against expectations you never defined.

slides.title: Week one decides the project
bullets: The decision the client will make with the data gets written down first - analysis without a decision is trivia.
Success criteria are defined as measurable checks: row counts, schema, sanity ranges - not vibes.
Every source gets profiled: quirks, cadence, edge cases, and the polite way to collect from it.
If scope is fuzzy, the first deliverable is clarity - a fixed written scope, not a running bill.

slides.title: Where scraping projects actually fail
slides.insight: The deadliest failure is silent: a scraper that exits zero and returns nothing - which is why every run validates row counts, schema, and sanity ranges.
slides.note: Illustrative incident mix consistent with the Web Scraping Toolkit design notes: tolerant extraction, fallbacks, and warnings over shrugs.

slides.title: Validation-first builds, loud failures
bullets: Every run validates row counts, schema, and sanity ranges before anything touches your dashboard.
Structured logs record what was fetched, what was skipped, and what was doubted - readable by humans, not terminal scrollback.
Failures report loudly; a scraper that silently returns empty data is worse than one that crashes.
Partial delivery with honest warnings beats silent perfectionism - you always know the state of your data.
slides.note: Do not trust a run because it exited zero; trust it because it passed checks you can read.

slides.title: Clarity climbs early; surprises burn down fast
slides.insight: Week one writes the definition of done, so clarity climbs immediately; surprises decay because bad news travels first and fast.
